resources.string: Your stance is stable and well balanced. Your body barely leans to either side, putting you in an ideal ready position to move quickly in any direction. Use this as the reliable starting point for every shot.

You\'re leaning side to side in your stance. Starting from an off-balance position throws off your base and makes your steps and swing harder to repeat consistently. Keep your hips and shoulders level and vertical, with your head stacked over your feet.

Your elbow reaches shoulder height in the trophy pose. Getting your elbow up to shoulder level gives the racket head more room to accelerate from there, which helps both the power and control of your serve. Aim to repeat this same height every time.

Your elbow isn\'t high enough in the trophy pose. A low elbow shortens the distance the racket has to accelerate, which costs you serve speed and puts extra strain on your shoulder. Look up at the toss and drive your elbow all the way up to shoulder height.
Your knee bend during the toss is well judged. A bend of roughly 130-150 degrees lets you drive off the ground and put your whole body\'s power into the serve.

Your knee bend is too shallow or too deep. Too shallow and you lose the leg drive that powers the serve, leaving it arm-only; too deep and your timing tends to fall apart. Sink into a comfortable 130-150 degree bend before you push up.
Your arm is fully extended at impact. Meeting the ball with the elbow nearly straight raises your contact point, which helps both the angle and the speed of your serve.

Your elbow isn\'t fully extended at impact. Contacting the ball with a bent elbow lowers your contact point, a common cause of hitting the net or losing pace. Toss slightly higher and reach all the way up so you meet the ball at full extension.
Your body tilt at impact is well judged. Stretching moderately up and toward the ball like this balances contact height with how well your body weight transfers into the shot.

Adjust your body tilt at impact. Staying too upright limits how high you reach, while leaning too far throws off your balance and control. Aim for a moderate forward stretch upward toward the ball, not straight up and not collapsed forward.
Your arm relaxes naturally through the follow-through. Letting go of tension after the swing makes it easier to reset for the next shot and reduces strain on your shoulder and elbow.

Your arm isn\'t relaxing fully. Staying tense after contact stiffens your motion and can lead to shoulder or elbow strain over time. Consciously release your arm right after impact and let the swing\'s own momentum carry it through.

Your arm swings all the way across your body on the follow-through. Finishing the swing fully lets the racket head accelerate through contact and lets natural forearm pronation happen, which also protects your arm.

Your follow-through is cut short. Stopping the swing early caps your racket-head speed and skips the natural pronation that both adds pace and protects your elbow. Let your arm swing all the way through to the opposite side of your body.
Your upper body rotates well through the unit turn. The clear gap between your shoulder and hip lines lets you unwind that stored rotation into a powerful, efficient swing.

Your upper body isn\'t rotating enough. A small gap between your shoulders and hips means you have no stored rotation to unwind, so you end up pushing the ball with just your arm, which costs both power and consistency. Turn your shoulders further back on the takeback to open a real gap against your hips.
You\'re meeting the ball well out in front of your body. Contacting it out front gives your arm room to swing freely through the ball, which helps both your power and your directional control.

You\'re contacting the ball too close to your body. Hitting it late and close cramps your swing, robbing you of power and making direction harder to control. Let the ball travel a little less before you hit it, meeting it further in front of your hips.
Your elbow angle at impact has good margin. Neither too cramped nor too straight, this angle absorbs impact well while still transferring power efficiently.

Your elbow is too cramped, or too straight, at impact. A cramped elbow chokes your swing, while a fully straight one can\'t absorb the shock and puts stress on your wrist and elbow. Adjust your distance to the ball so your elbow keeps a comfortable amount of bend at contact.
You swing all the way through to over your shoulder. Completing the swing this fully lets you use the racket head\'s full acceleration, which keeps your spin and control consistent.

Your finish is cut short. Stopping the swing partway wastes the racket head\'s acceleration and tends to leave you short on spin and pace. Keep swinging without decelerating after contact, all the way through to over your shoulder.
Your lower body is leading the turn well. Starting the rotation from your hips takes unnecessary tension out of your upper body while still producing plenty of stable power.

Your lower body isn\'t turning enough. Twisting mostly from the upper body is harder to repeat and caps how much power you can generate. On the takeback, start the rotation from your hips first and let your shoulders follow.
Both elbow angles are stable at impact. Keeping this compact arm shape transfers your body rotation straight into the racket and keeps your contact point consistent.

Your elbow angles break down at impact. Letting your arms overextend or collapse breaks the connection between your body turn and the racket, and your contact point drifts around. Keep a compact triangle shape with both arms through contact.
Your chest rotates well through the finish. Turning your body fully toward the target lets you use all of your rotational power right through to the end of the swing.

Your body isn\'t rotating enough at the finish. Stopping the rotation partway leaves power on the table and shifts the load onto your arm alone. Keep turning your chest toward the target after contact instead of stopping the rotation early.
Your one-handed backhand unit turn looks good. Turning your shoulder fully on the takeback sets you up to unleash that stored rotation into a sharp, powerful swing.

You\'re not rotating enough on the takeback. A shallow shoulder turn means you have no stored rotation to release, so you end up pushing the ball with your arm alone. Turn your shoulder fully on the takeback so your body is closed to the target before you swing.
You\'re keeping your torso from opening up too early at impact. Because your chest hasn\'t turned to face the target yet, your racket face stays square through contact.

Your body is opening up too much at impact. When your chest turns to face the target too early, the racket face opens with it and the ball tends to float or drift wide. Hold your chest sideways a little longer and delay opening it until just after contact.
Your elbow is locked in and stable at impact. Keeping your arm extended like this transfers your body\'s rotational power into the racket with no energy lost along the way.

Your elbow isn\'t stable at impact. Meeting the ball with a bent elbow absorbs the shock poorly and loses power on the way to the racket. Extend your arm fully into contact so the elbow locks and stays stable.
You swing all the way through to the finish. Completing the swing fully brings out the sharp spin and power that a one-handed backhand can generate.

Your swing is cut short. Stopping partway through keeps you from getting the spin and power a one-handed backhand is capable of. Keep swinging without slowing down after contact, all the way through to the finish.
